rationale: B wins because it keeps the strongest stories inside the supplied facts and makes the missing proof impossible to ignore. Its "Donors, not districts, are paying for the AI tutor headed to 1 million more students" is a real money-and-sustainability angle; A's "while rivals still charge for it" wanders into competitor contrast without evidence. A has usable bones, especially the non-peer-reviewed study angle, but B is the one a founder could take into a newsroom conversation without carrying a bag of invented premises.
gaps_in_A: "while rivals still charge for it" is an invented market contrast. The update says Khanmigo is donor-funded and free to teachers; it does not say commercial rivals charge, how much, or that the market is splitting that way.
"which tends to center on students" is unsupported coverage history. If you claim the teacher feature has been overlooked, bring clips or cut the aside.

"Free AI lesson-planning help arrives for teachers already stretched thin" leans on a teacher-workload premise the update does not supply. It becomes pitchable only with time-saved data or teacher testimony, which A admits it lacks.
"Next step: fact-check" is too narrow. The set also needs donor economics, named districts, and on-record educators before most of these angles can leave the building.
gaps_in_B: "What one pilot district saw when students used an AI tutor regularly" is the weakest kept angle because no district is named. It is a useful reporting target, but not a pitchable story until Khan gives a real district, person, and district-level result.

"The district is joining the rollout, or its pilot results are part of what is being published now" blurs two different stories. A new-district adoption story and a pilot-results story need different proof and different local hooks.
"Next step: journalist-fit-check" jumps one beat too far. The actual next move is asset collection: full methodology, donor terms, named districts, and on-record critics or teachers.
